title: Cornish Pasty
subtitle: Raw beef skirt, swede, potato, and onion in a crimped shortcrust
excerpt: A Cornish pasty is a sealed shortcrust pastry parcel filled with raw beef skirt, thinly sliced swede, potato, and onion, crimped down one side and baked. The ingredients go in raw and cook together inside the pastry. The traditional crimp runs along the top; the D-shape is essential to the identity of the dish.
sourceNotes: The Cornish pasty holds Protected Geographical Indication (PGI) status in the UK. Traditional recipes specify skirt steak, swede (not turnip), and a top crimp. The dish has been associated with the mines and agriculture of Cornwall for at least two centuries.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze unbaked pasties on a tray, then transfer to bags. Bake from frozen at 180°C fan for 50 to 55 minutes.
recipe.batchNotes: Make a double batch and freeze half. They reheat well from frozen.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Assemble and refrigerate up to 12 hours before baking.

glossaryTerms.definition: To pinch or fold the edge of a pastry parcel to seal it and create a decorative rope-like edge. On a Cornish pasty, the crimp runs along the top.

content.text: A Cornish pasty is a self-contained meal: thinly sliced swede, potato, and onion with raw skirt steak, seasoned generously and sealed in shortcrust pastry. The filling cooks inside the pastry during baking, absorbing the meat juices as it goes. The
along the top (not the edge) is the traditional mark of the Cornish version and makes the pasty easy to hold and eat out of hand.

attrs.title: Skirt steak and swede
attrs.body: Skirt steak (also called beef skirt) is the traditional cut; it is flavourful and cooks tender inside the pastry. If you cannot find it, use beef chuck cut very thin. Swede, not turnip, is the correct root vegetable for an authentic Cornish pasty.

items.prepNote: cut into very thin 1 cm slices (skirt steak is traditional)
peeled and thinly sliced, about 3 mm

content.text: Season the sliced vegetables and meat generously before assembling. The filling goes in raw with no pre-cooking. The small piece of butter per pasty melts into the filling and helps build the gravy.
Divide the pastry into 4 equal pieces. On a lightly floured surface, roll each piece into a circle about 25 cm across and 3 mm thick. Use a plate as a guide if needed.

On one half of each circle, layer the sliced swede, then the sliced potato, then the sliced onion, and finally the thin beef slices. Season each layer well with salt and pepper. Lay a small piece of butter on top. Leave a 2 cm border clear around the edge.

Brush the border with beaten egg. Fold the empty half of the pastry over the filling to make a D-shape. Press the edges together firmly, then twist and fold the edge into a rope crimp along the top curved edge. Make sure the seal is tight. Cut a small steam hole in the top. Brush with beaten egg.

Heat the oven to 200°C fan. Place the pasties on a lined baking tray. Bake for 20 minutes until the pastry is set and starting to colour, then reduce to 180°C fan for a further 35 minutes. The filling cooks through in this time. Leave to rest for 5 minutes before eating.

items.symptom: The pastry splits open during baking
items.cause: The filling expanded as it steamed and the crimp was not sealed tightly enough.
items.fix: Press the edges firmly before crimping and make sure there are no gaps. A tight crimp along the top, rather than a thin pinch, holds better.

items.symptom: The swede is still hard after baking
items.fix: Swede needs to be sliced thinly, 2 to 3 mm at most, to cook through in the time the pastry takes to bake.

items.symptom: The pastry is pale and soft
items.cause: The oven temperature dropped during baking, or the tray was on a low shelf.
items.fix: Bake on the middle shelf. If the pasties are pale after 55 minutes, raise the temperature to 200°C for the final 5 minutes.

items.cause: The butter was omitted, or the meat was too lean.
items.fix: Include the small piece of butter per pasty. It melts into the filling and combines with the meat juices to make a small, savoury gravy.

content.text: The Cornish pasty has Protected Geographical Indication status. Only pasties made to the traditional recipe in Cornwall can legally use the name. The dish has been part of Cornish working life for over two centuries. Miners and farm workers carried it as a portable lunch that needed no cutlery. The thick crimp served as a handle, traditionally discarded rather than eaten.
